questions.q: Which database does @zudojs/database support?
questions.explain: The package is built on Prisma and supports PostgreSQL only. PGlite is PostgreSQL itself, running inside Node.js, which is why the lesson can use it for learning.
options: Any SQL database: PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite
PostgreSQL only
Only PGlite, never a PostgreSQL server
MongoDB and PostgreSQL

questions.q: ZudoJS talks to a PrismaClientLike object. What does it need from that object?
questions.explain: Anything that has those five methods works. That is the adapter pattern: a small object that makes one thing (PGlite, or a real Prisma client) look like what ZudoJS expects.
options: A generated model for every table, and nothing else
A connection string it can open by itself
A few methods: $connect, $disconnect, $queryRawUnsafe, $executeRawUnsafe and $transaction
An instance of the pg driver's Pool class

questions.q: In the lesson's whereToSql, values become $1, $2… parameters, but field names are checked against an allow-list instead. Why?
questions.explain: Parameters can only stand for values. A column name is part of the SQL text itself, so it must come from a fixed list of names you trust. Anything else is refused.
options: Allow-lists are faster than parameters
Parameters only work for numbers, not text
A field (column) name cannot be a SQL parameter, so the only safe way is to accept known names only
PostgreSQL ignores unknown columns, so the check is only for nicer errors

questions.q: The PGlite adapter turns PostgreSQL error 23505 into the Prisma code P2002. What does 23505 mean?
questions.explain: 23505 is a unique violation. ZudoJS understands the Prisma code P2002 and turns it into a 409 Conflict. A missing row becomes P2025, which ZudoJS turns into 404.
options: The row you asked for was not found
A unique value is already used (a UNIQUE rule was broken)
The SQL has a syntax error
The connection timed out

questions.q: Where should a connection string like postgres://app:pa55@db:5432/tasks come from?
questions.explain: It contains a password, so it is a secret: read it from the environment, never write it in code. Checking it at start-up makes a missing setting fail loudly at once, not at the first request.
options: A constant at the top of database.ts, so it is easy to find
An environment variable such as DATABASE_URL, checked when the app starts
The request, so each client can choose its database
A comment in the README, copied into the code when you deploy

questions.q: Your start-up check finds that DATABASE_URL does not start with postgres://. Which error message is best?
questions.explain: The message should name the setting and the problem, but never show the value. Error messages end up in logs, and the value contains a password.
options: DATABASE_URL is invalid: mysql://root:hunter2@db/tasks
DATABASE_URL must start with postgres://
Error
No message: just call process.exit(1)

questions.q: Finish requireDatabaseUrl(env). Throw a ConfigurationError with the message DATABASE_URL is not set when it is missing or empty, and DATABASE_URL must start with postgres:// when it starts with anything other than postgres:// or postgresql://. Otherwise return the URL. Never put the value in a message.
questions.explain: Check for a missing value first, then the format, with a regular expression such as /^postgres(ql)?:\/\//. The messages name the setting but never repeat the value, which may contain a password.
questions.expected:
ConfigurationError - DATABASE_URL is not set
ConfigurationError - DATABASE_URL must start with postgres://
ok: postgresql://db/tasks

questions.q: This runs the same migration list twice against PGlite. What does it print?
questions.explain: The runner records every applied migration in its _migrations table. The second migrate() sees both versions there and skips them, so it applies nothing and never runs CREATE TABLE again.
options: The second run fails: relation "tasks" already exists

questions.q: Migration 1 already ran on the shared staging database. You need one more column in tasks. What do you do?
questions.explain: An applied migration is frozen. The runner only looks at version numbers, so an edited migration 1 would never run again anywhere it already ran. A new migration (version 3) runs everywhere, in order.
options: Edit migration 1 to add the column and run migrate() again
Delete the row for version 1 from _migrations, then edit migration 1
Add a new migration with the next version number that adds the column
Run the ALTER TABLE by hand in the database console

questions.q: Two copies of your server start at the same moment and both call migrate(). What stops them from applying the same migration twice?
questions.explain: An advisory lock lets only one runner work at a time. When the second one gets the lock, the _migrations table already lists the migrations, so it skips them.
options: Nothing: you must start the servers one by one
The runner takes a PostgreSQL advisory lock while it works, so the second copy waits and then skips what is done
PostgreSQL refuses the second CREATE TABLE, and the error is ignored
The runner keeps its history in memory, shared by both processes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Like migrations, seeds are recorded (in a _seeds table) and run only once. The second run skipped default-roles, so there are still 2 roles, not 4.
options: [ 'default-roles' ] 2
[ 'default-roles' ] 4

questions.q: An attacker types nothing' OR '1'='1 into the search box. What does this print?
questions.explain: In the string-built query, the attacker's quote ends the string and OR '1'='1' is always true, so every row comes back. With $1, the whole input is one plain value, and no task has that odd title.

questions.q: Finish whereEquals(filter, fields). For each key of filter, check it is in fields (throw TypeError("Unknown field") otherwise) and add "key" = $n, with the value pushed to params. Join the parts with AND . Return { sql, params }. Values must never go into the SQL text.
questions.explain: Field names come from an allow-list; values only ever appear as $1, $2… with the real values in params. params.push() returns the new length, which is the number of the next parameter.
questions.expected:
{ sql: '"done" = $1 AND "priority" = $2', params: [ false, 'high' ] }
TypeError Unknown field

questions.q: What is a repository?
questions.explain: A repository keeps all the queries for one table in one place. Routes and services call methods like findByTitle and never see SQL.
options: A folder of SQL files
One class that owns all access to one table; the rest of the app asks it for data and never writes SQL
A copy of the database used for backups
The npm registry where @zudojs/database is published

questions.q: The fake delegate below throws the Prisma error P2002 (unique value already used). What does this print?
questions.explain: The repository maps P2002 to a DatabaseError with status 409 Conflict. The message is generic on purpose: it never repeats the database's own text, which could name constraints and tables.
options: 409 Task already exists. true
500 duplicate key value false
400 Task already exists. false
409 duplicate key value true

questions.q: The fake delegate below throws P2025 (record not found). What does this print?
questions.explain: Updating a row that does not exist becomes a 404 with the code ERR_NOT_FOUND. Your API's error handler can pass that status on as it is.
options: 404 ERR_NOT_FOUND true
500 P2025 false
409 ERR_CONFLICT false
404 P2025 true

questions.q: The fake delegate records the arguments the repository sends it. What does this print?
questions.explain: With softDelete: true, every read adds deletedAt: null, so soft-deleted rows are skipped. Use findDeleted() or withDeleted() when you really want to see them.
options: {"AND":[{"done":false},{"deletedAt":null}]}
{"done":false}
{"done":false,"deletedAt":{"not":null}}
{"deletedAt":null}

questions.q: A support tool must count all tasks, including soft-deleted ones. Which call does that?
questions.explain: withDeleted() returns a copy of the repository that sees every row. Plain count() skips deleted rows, and findDeleted() lists only the deleted ones.
options: tasks.count()
tasks.findDeleted()
tasks.withDeleted().count()
tasks.count({ deletedAt: null })

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The query builder never writes SQL. It produces a plain Prisma-style object; the repository hands it to the delegate, and the adapter turns it into SQL with parameters. limit(10) becomes skip: 0, take: 10.
options: {"where":{"done":{"equals":false},"title":{"contains":"milk"}},"orderBy":[{"id":"desc"}],"skip":0,"take":10}
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE done = false AND title LIKE '%milk%' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 10
{"where":{"done":false,"title":"milk"},"orderBy":{"id":"desc"},"limit":10}
{"where":{"done":{"equals":false},"title":{"contains":"milk"}},"orderBy":[{"id":"desc"}],"take":10}

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Page 3 with 5 per page skips the first two pages: (3 − 1) × 5 = 10 rows, then takes 5.

questions.q: The lesson's tasks include Call the bank and The weekly report. Which does whereContains("title", "the") match?
questions.explain: whereContains is case-sensitive: "the" does not match "The".
options: Only Call the bank, because the match is case-sensitive
Both, because contains ignores case
Neither, because contains needs the whole title
Only The weekly report, because it starts with the word

questions.q: A client sends ?sort=title; DROP TABLE tasks. What does this print?
questions.explain: ZudoJS checks sort fields before they reach the database and refuses any name that is not a plain identifier. The delegate is never called. In a real route, also check the field against a short allow-list and answer 400.
options: TypeError Invalid query field name "title; DROP TABLE tasks".
query sent
DatabaseError Unknown field "title; DROP TABLE tasks"
SyntaxError Unexpected token ";"

questions.q: Finish parseSort(text) for GET /tasks?sort=…. A leading - means descending. Only id, title and createdAt are allowed. Return { status: 200, sort: { field, direction } }, or { status: 400 } for any other field.
questions.explain: Check the client's choice against a short list of allowed fields and answer 400 for anything else. password is a valid name, but not one the client may sort by.

questions.q: When is keyset (cursor) pagination the better choice?
questions.explain: Keyset pagination asks for "the rows after the last one I saw". It stays fast on huge tables and does not skip or repeat rows when new ones are added. Offset pagination is the one for page numbers.
options: When users need to jump straight to page 50
When you need the total number of pages
For "load more" and infinite scrolling on big tables, where new rows keep arriving
Only for tables with fewer than 100 rows

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 25 rows with 10 per page need 3 pages (the last one holds 5). Page 3 is the last, so there is no next page, but there is a previous one.
options: 3 false true
2 true true
3 true true
2 false true

questions.q: Finish pageInfo(page, limit, total). Return { offset, totalPages, hasNext }: offset is how many rows to skip, totalPages is rounded up, and hasNext says whether a later page exists.
questions.explain: Skip (page - 1) * limit rows. Use Math.ceil so a half-full last page still counts. There is a next page while page < totalPages.

questions.q: The first part of a cursor, before the dot, is the position in Base64. What does this print?
questions.explain: Base64 is not encryption: anyone can read the position. That is why the second part, the signature, matters: it proves the server made this cursor.
options: {"page":2}
nySv_IOv5J-S0Pqx2wp7NtmJoZLgIR3kP0ZwbiFLgRY

questions.q: A cursor signed with one secret is checked with another. What does this print?
questions.explain: With the right secret the position comes back. Any change, or another secret, breaks the signature and the cursor is refused. A cursor travels through the client, so signing it is what makes a forged one detectable.
options:
{ id: 2 }
refused: Invalid pagination cursor signature.

eyJpZCI6Mn0
refused: Invalid pagination cursor signature.

questions.q: A client sends a forged cursor, and paginateCursor refuses it with a ValidationError. What status should the client get?
questions.explain: A bad cursor is the client's mistake, so the answer is 400. The ValidationError already carries status 400, so your error handler can pass it on as it is. Answering 500 would wrongly say the server is broken, and quietly returning page 1 hides the problem.
options: 500 Internal Server Error, because the query failed
400 Bad Request, because the bad cursor is the client's mistake
200 with page 1, as if no cursor was sent
200 with an empty list

questions.q: The callback inserts a row, then throws. What does this print?
questions.explain: withTransaction commits only if the callback returns. It threw, so the insert was rolled back: all-or-nothing.
options:
transaction failed
rows: 0

transaction failed
rows: 1
rows: 1
rows: 0

questions.q: Inside a withTransaction callback, how should you use the tasks repository?
questions.explain: A query through the ordinary tasks repository runs outside the transaction, so it would not be rolled back. The tx-bound copy makes every query part of it.
options: Use tasks as usual; every query joins the open transaction by itself
Use tasks.withTransaction(tx), a copy bound to the transaction, for every query in the callback
Create a new database client inside the callback
Call tasks.softDelete() first, to lock the table

questions.q: When does withTransactionRetry(client, callback, { retries: 3 }) run the callback again?
questions.explain: Serialization failures and deadlocks are safe to retry: running the whole callback again usually succeeds. A validation error would fail the same way every time, so it is not retried.
options: After any error, including your own validation errors
When PostgreSQL reports a serialization failure or a deadlock, errors that mean "try again"
Every time, three times, to be sure the data is saved
Only when the network is down

questions.q: Finish healthRoute(check). check is an async function that returns { healthy, status, message }. Answer { status: 200 } or { status: 503 }, with a body { database: … } that holds only the status text. Never put message in the body: a health endpoint is public.
questions.explain: Answer 503 when the database is down, so a load balancer stops sending traffic. The error message names an internal host and port, so it stays in your logs and out of the public body.
questions.expected:
{ status: 200, body: { database: 'healthy' } }
{ status: 503, body: { database: 'unhealthy' } }

questions.q: During start-up, before migrations are done, what should the server report?
questions.explain: Health (liveness) asks "is this process working?". Readiness asks "can it take traffic right now?". A server running its migrations is working but cannot serve requests yet.
options: Not alive and not ready
Alive (healthy) but not ready
Ready but not alive
Alive and ready

questions.q: With Prisma in production, where do you set the connection pool size (max)?
questions.explain: The pool belongs to the driver adapter, not to @zudojs/database. Start with about 10 per server process, and remember that PostgreSQL has a total limit shared by all your servers.
options: In createDatabaseClient's options
In the driver adapter, new PrismaPg({ connectionString, max: 10 })
In the migration runner
PostgreSQL chooses it; you cannot set it

questions.q: A PATCH body may leave fields out, and a form may send undefined. Finish updateSql(id, data): skip keys whose value is undefined (they mean "leave it"), and build UPDATE tasks SET "field" = $1, … WHERE "id" = $n with the values in params and the id last. Return { sql, params }.
questions.explain: Filter out undefined first, like Prisma does: otherwise the title would be set to NULL. params.push(value) returns the new length, which is the right $ number. (In a real app, field names also go through an allow-list.)
questions.expected:
UPDATE tasks SET "done" = $1, "priority" = $2 WHERE "id" = $3 [ true, 'high', 4 ]
UPDATE tasks SET "title" = $1 WHERE "id" = $2 [ 'Pack bags', 7 ]

questions.q: Migration 3 adds a due_date column. You then call tasks.update(1, { dueDate: "2026-10-01" }) and get Unknown field "dueDate". What did you forget?
questions.explain: The adapter only accepts field names in TASK_MODEL.fields. A new column needs its field name added there (and to the Task type), or the allow-list refuses it.
options: To run migrate() a second time
To add "dueDate" to TASK_MODEL.fields, the adapter's allow-list
To restart PostgreSQL
To write a seed for the new column

questions.q: The seed created all five tasks in one transaction, so they share the same createdAt. How do you make "newest first" a stable order?
questions.explain: When two rows have the same createdAt, the order between them is not fixed. A unique second sort field such as id breaks the tie. Without ORDER BY, PostgreSQL promises no order at all.
options: Sort by title instead
Sort by createdAt descending, then by id descending as a second field
Remove orderBy; PostgreSQL returns rows in insert order
Add a random number column and sort by it

questions.q: Clients send ?page=2&limit=5000. What does the practice's listTasks do with limit=5000?
questions.explain: Query-string values are text and come from the client, so validate them: schema.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(50). A limit that is too big is refused with 400, so no one can ask for the whole table.
options: It returns all rows, because the client asked for them
It quietly uses 50 instead
The schema (limit 1 to 50) rejects it, and the route answers 400
It passes 5000 to the database, which caps it at 100

questions.q: The fake delegate prints what the repository asks for. What does this print?
questions.explain: Normal reads skip deleted rows (deletedAt: null). withDeleted() removes that filter and sees everything. findDeleted() asks for only the rows whose deletedAt is set.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Page 3 with 2 per page skips 4 items, so only 'e' is left. It is the last page, so hasNextPage is false.
options: [ 'e' ] 5 false
[ 'e', undefined ] 5 false
[ 'c', 'd' ] 5 true
[] 5 false

questions.q: In a LIKE pattern, % and _ are wildcards and \ escapes. Finish containsPattern(text): put a \ before every \, % and _ in the user's text, then wrap it in %…%. The result is sent as a $1 parameter, so a search for 100% finds only titles that really contain 100%.
questions.explain: The lesson's adapter does the same: text.replace(/[\\%_]/g, "\\$&"). $& is the matched character. Without it, 100% would match every title that starts with 100.

questions.q: Finish column(field, fields), like the lesson's adapter. If field is not in fields, throw new TypeError(`Unknown field "${field}"`). Otherwise turn camelCase into snake_case and wrap it in double quotes: createdAt becomes "created_at".
questions.explain: Check the allow-list first, before the name goes near SQL. Then replace each capital letter with _ and its lower-case form.

questions.q: Migration 1 succeeds. Migration 2 inserts a row, then throws. What state is the database in afterwards?
questions.explain: Each migration runs in its own transaction. If one fails halfway, its changes are undone and the ones before it stay. The next migrate() tries migration 2 again.
options: Nothing changed: migration 1 is undone too
Migration 1 stays applied (version 1); migration 2's insert is rolled back and it is still pending
Both are applied, including migration 2's row
Migration 2 is marked applied, but its row is missing

questions.q: The database is down. What should GET /health answer, using checkDatabaseHealth?
questions.explain: An honest health route makes the load balancer stop sending traffic to a server that cannot answer. The endpoint is public, so the body names only the status; details go to the logs.
options: 200 with { database: "ok" }, because the process itself is running
503 Service Unavailable with { database: "unhealthy" }, and no error text or host name in the body
500 with the full error message, so operators can see it
404, because the database was not found
